title: How much would it realistically cost, and how long would it take, to create a 2-3 hour story-driven RPG almost entirely with AI and zero coding experience?
author: Asleep-Sprinkles2880
selftext:
I've been thinking about developing my own game, and I'm curious how realistic it would be to create a complete, polished game almost entirely with AI, starting with absolutely no programming or game development experience.

I'm not talking about generating a game with a single prompt and expecting AI to do everything automatically. I understand that game development requires a lot of work, and I'm prepared to be actively involved throughout the entire process.

# The Game Concept

My idea is to create a relatively short, story-driven RPG where **a single playthrough of the main story would take approximately 2-3 hours**.

The game would be heavily focused on storytelling, exploration, character interactions, moral dilemmas, and meaningful player choices rather than combat, grinding, farming, or character progression.

Ideally, I'd like to have around 10 different endings, with the player's decisions throughout the story influencing which ending they receive.

However, I'm not planning to create 10 entirely separate storylines. The idea is to have a central narrative with branching events, consequences, alternative scenes, and different outcomes based on the player's actions.

**The story would be the main attraction. Combat and boss fights would exist to complement the narrative, not dominate the gameplay.**

# 1. Main World Top-Down RPG (80-90% of Gameplay)

Most of the game would be a traditional 2D top-down RPG focused on:

* Exploring locations, towns, and environments.
* Interacting with NPCs and having meaningful conversations.
* Completing story-driven quests and discovering secrets.
* Making decisions that affect characters, relationships, future events, and the world itself.
* Encountering regular enemies with relatively simple combat mechanics.
* Experiencing a branching narrative where previous decisions influence how the story develops.

I don't want the game to revolve around grinding experience, farming resources, repetitive combat, or spending hours improving character stats.

Instead, I want the player to progress naturally through the story, with exploration and interactions being the primary gameplay elements.

# 2. Boss Fights Side-View Action RPG / Soulslike

Although the game would primarily focus on its story, I'd still like major boss encounters to feel unique and mechanically engaging.

When the player encounters a significant boss, the gameplay would transition from the top-down perspective into a separate 2D side-view combat arena.

These encounters would feature:

* Real-time combat with precise movement and timing.
* Dodging, stamina management, and parrying.
* Attack combinations and special abilities.
* Bosses with multiple phases and unique attack patterns.
* Fast-paced combat inspired by Hollow Knight and Soulslike games.

However, **boss fights wouldn't be the main focus of the game**.

I'd rather have a small number of memorable, story-relevant boss encounters than dozens of repetitive fights.

Each boss would ideally serve a narrative purpose, and defeating them could lead to important decisions that affect the story.

The goal isn't to create an extremely difficult game focused on mastering combat mechanics. I just want boss encounters to provide a meaningful change of pace and feel exciting when they happen.

# 3. AI-Generated Cinematics and Player Choices

Another important feature I'd like to implement is AI-generated animated cinematic cutscenes.

For example, after defeating a boss, an AI-generated video sequence would play.

At a specific moment, the cinematic would stop, and the player would be presented with a decision, such as killing the boss, sparing them, or making some kind of agreement.

Depending on the player's choice, a different cinematic sequence would play, and the decision would influence future events, NPC interactions, quests, or even the ending.

These would be pre-generated video sequences integrated into the game, not videos generated in real time during gameplay.

I imagine using these cinematics primarily for important story moments rather than every interaction or encounter.

# 4. How I'd Like to Develop It

My goal is to create the game almost entirely using AI tools, without hiring a traditional development team.

I'd like to rely heavily on AI for:

* **Programming:** Using AI to write, explain, debug, and improve code while I handle implementation, testing, and feedback.
* **Characters and assets:** Using AI image generation and image-to-2D/3D tools to create characters, NPCs, enemies, items, environments, and other game assets. Ideally, I'd like tools that can transform reference images into usable sprites, models, or other game-ready assets with minimal manual modeling.
* **Animations:** Using AI-assisted tools to create animations for characters, enemies, bosses, and environmental elements.
* **Cinematics:** Generating animated cutscenes with AI video tools, including alternative sequences based on player decisions.
* **Audio:** Using AI tools where appropriate for sound effects, voices, and other audio elements.
* **Game systems:** Using AI assistance to develop dialogue systems, quest tracking, inventory, combat mechanics, boss behavior, save systems, and branching narrative logic.

I'm especially interested in tools or workflows where I could generate a character image, turn it into a usable 2D or 3D asset, animate it, and import it into a game engine without having to create everything manually.

I understand that AI-generated assets aren't necessarily game-ready and that considerable work may still be required to integrate and refine them.

My role would essentially be that of the game's designer, writer, director, and tester.

I'd develop the story, design the mechanics, make creative decisions, guide the AI, test the results, identify problems, and continuously improve the game.

I'm willing to spend serious time learning whatever is necessary along the way, but I'd like AI to handle as much of the technical production as realistically possible.

# 5. My Main Questions

1. **How much would developing a game like this realistically cost?** I'm specifically interested in out-of-pocket expenses for AI subscriptions, generation credits, development tools, assets, and other necessary services, assuming I'm doing the work myself rather than hiring developers.
2. **How long would development realistically take?** Considering that the main story would take approximately 2–3 hours to complete, with multiple possible endings, and that I'd be starting with no programming or game development experience.
3. **How practical is AI-generated asset creation today?** Are there reliable tools that can turn images into usable 2D sprites, animations, or 3D models without requiring extensive manual work? How difficult is maintaining visual consistency?
4. **Can AI realistically help develop both gameplay systems?** A relatively simple top-down RPG for exploration and story progression, with a separate, more advanced side-view combat system specifically for boss encounters.
5. **How difficult would it be to implement branching AI-generated cinematics?** Particularly sequences that stop at predetermined moments, present player choices, and continue with different pre-generated videos depending on the decision.
6. **Would keeping the game relatively short and heavily story-focused significantly reduce development costs and complexity?** Especially compared to a traditional RPG with extensive combat, leveling systems, farming, and a much longer campaign.
7. **What are the biggest limitations of AI-assisted game development?** Which parts would still require substantial programming knowledge, artistic skills, or manual work?
8. **Has anyone actually attempted something similar?** I'd be particularly interested in real examples, development timelines, money spent, problems encountered, and whether the final result was worth the effort.

# What I'm Trying to Figure Out

To clarify, I'm not trying to develop a massive open-world RPG or a game with dozens of hours of content.

**I'm aiming for a relatively short but polished, narrative-focused experience that takes around 2-3 hours to finish on a single playthrough, with enough meaningful choices and alternative outcomes to encourage replaying it.**

I'd rather create a smaller game with a compelling story, memorable characters, impactful decisions, and a few well-designed boss encounters than a much larger game filled with repetitive content.

I'm also not expecting AI to magically create everything with a few prompts.

I'm prepared to spend a significant amount of time directing the project, learning, experimenting, integrating assets, testing mechanics, fixing problems, and refining the final result.

What I'm trying to understand is how much AI can realistically reduce the financial and technical barriers to solo game development today.

**Is creating a complete, polished, 2–3 hour story-driven RPG with these features realistically achievable for one person with no prior programming experience, using AI as their primary development tool?**

**And if so, what would be a reasonable estimate for the total out-of-pocket cost and development time?**

I'd really appreciate honest answers from experienced developers and people who have actually experimented with AI-assisted game development.

I'm not looking for AI hype or unrealistic promises. I'm genuinely interested in understanding what's currently possible, what isn't, and how much work a project like this would actually require.

comments.author: Tom_Baron
comments.body:
Any llm will sketch out the game you describe to start with, you cant convey everything you want in text in even the first 100 prompts. 

The sketch will be totally generic till you choose otherwise, a nod to how the tool works. Your game will likely work if you try prompt the whole thing. I like doing this, you get an early impression with some imagination whether the idea works in practice.

Its up to you then to paint the game you want, adding detail to each part of the initial draft.

That can take a while. My game was playable in two hours, ive lost track of time now. I think my first commit was a month ago, im into 1000s of prompts with two models 50 commits or so, creating 4-5 hours a day into the early hours after my job/parenting commitments are done 🤣 and im no where near finished!

comments.author: cdcox
comments.body:
There's no universal answer. It depends on how well you work with the tools and how complicated the game you want to make is going to be. You could snap out a prototype in an afternoon. But a quality protptype could be a week. Could be months. You probably won't have anything polished inside 3 months unless this is like your full-time commitment. But for instance, making a cheap little RPG Maker game that accomplishes your goal could take very little time. Making a full-on unity game with complicated mechanics where you have to spin everything yourself with complicated 16 bit graphics could take a very long time. It really depends what you want to make and how big you want it to be. 3 hours could mean almost anything.

The best way to figure it out though is to just test.

First come up with a design document the list s: approximately how many bosses, how many NPCS, how many backgrounds , how many scenes. It doesn't have to be perfect but get as close to range as you can imagine this will help you figure out how much of the following behaviors you need to do:

Next, come up with a concept for a boss. Work out every move the boss is going to do, figure out how many frames each of those moves is going to be. Then try to generate in those frames and moves and see how long it takes you. Some people are wizards and very skilled at frame interpolation and skeletonizing and can pull something like that in an afternoon some people it'll take days. See how long it takes you and then multiply it by the number of bosses. You'll get better as it goes on but to polish. You'll probably have to redo a fair number of them.

Do the same thing with a side character sprite. Multiply by the number of side characters 

Figure out based off the number of animations you're making  how many animations the main character will be and use that to estimate how long the main character will take. 

For generating videos, if you've not done it a lot, it'll take a long time just to learn how to. This will probably be one of the more expensive and time consuming things in your whole process. That being said, branching storylines is very easy with AI videos because you can use the final frame of your branch point as the start of the next video so you can easily set that up. But like the sprites take it toy example and try to generate it in seedance, kling, hy3, or a few others. Generate the start frame you want and try to direct the video to get where you want it to go. Some people are wizards at this and can pull 5-minute videos in a day for under a few bucks. Some people will take weeks to get a single 30-second clip and tens or hundreds of dollars. See where you lie. Once you get a video you're happy with multiply that by the number of videos you need to generate.

And then do the same with dialogue. Try writing a couple scenes. See how long it takes. Multiply by the number of scenes you have to write out. Then realize you're writing way too much and double the time so you can spend the second half cutting down your writing to a punchy moment.

Ironically, I think the code is probably going to be the fastest part. I know you want to write the code on your own,  that'll be way slower. But if you really want to do it, I'd double whatever your above combined estimate is because every single asset needs to be wired and tweaked and optimized. You probably don't need more than a pro subscription for the number of months you're working though unless you're just letting agents free run all over your system, which it doesn't sound like you really need for the type of game you're making.

So take all the above and add it up and check your token costs. Check your time and then you have a good estimate. Double everything just because that's how it goes when you're trying to make something. It'll take you less than a 10th of the time/cost of the whole game to figure out how long it'll take to make the whole game and determine if it's feasible within your budget and timeline. If you can't do that much work to get the estimate then either you really shouldn't be making a game because all the stuff I listed above is exactly what you'll need to do to over and over to make the game or you really want to make this game no matter what the time or cost, so who cares just make the game.

comments.author: magicdoorai
comments.body:
The feature list is closer to two games sharing a story than one short RPG: a top-down exploration system and a timing-sensitive side-view boss fighter. The perspective switch, animation states, save/load across branches and testing every choice are likely to dominate the schedule, not the 2-3 hour playtime. AI can help write a prototype, but it won't decide whether the parry feels fair or whether ten endings remain coherent.

I'd price this with a vertical slice rather than a whole-game estimate: one room, one NPC with a choice that persists after reload, one boss with a single phase, and one pre-rendered cutscene that branches into two short clips. Use placeholder art first. Track hours of prompting, debugging, manual asset cleanup, and playtesting separately from subscription fees and generation credits. If that slice is fun and stable, extrapolate from measured effort, not from a model's optimistic timeline.

Pre-rendered branching video is technically straightforward to switch at a fixed point; making matching characters/lighting/continuity across alternate clips and revisions is the expensive part. A still illustration plus text for most branches can save a lot of re-generation. I wouldn't commit to ten endings or paid video batches before you've shipped and tested the one-choice slice.

comments.author: StarMonkeyGames
comments.body:
That is A LOT of text. I used AI to summarize it. 

\-------------------

Can someone with zero coding experience use AI to make a polished, 2–3 hour story-driven RPG with branching endings, Soulslike boss fights, and AI-generated cinematics?

How much would it cost, how long would it take, and what are the biggest challenges?

  
\-------------------

Yes, AI can code pretty much whatever you need now. I'm an engineer. Brother is an engineer. Wife is an engineer. The corporate world has moved on. Anyone saying it can't is lying. All your software will be made by AI in the next few years. We all know that it's going to be able to provide quality assets. 

But from what I noticed. Even if you throw money at the problem. Most of the AI games I've seen end in prototype. In the past, most game dev journeys ended at hello world phase. Now most are ending at the prototype phase. It's like the barrier has gone down, but there are still plenty of other hurdles, even after the prototype.   


Anyway, the thing about zero code experience. I think you should at least do a crash course on object oriented programming. There are plenty of youtube game series on this I bet. 

AI will code for you, but it can't read your mind. And it's not like perfect all the time. And when you screw up and misprompt, it doesn't care. Like here is an example

  
I have a project with a dedicated animation manager. That means, anything that is rendering related, it should use this thing.   
  
Then I'll be like "I want this new feature to the AI" and it will be like got it boss. Then it will make me the feature, but it will also create a separate mini rendering mechanic on the new thing. And it becomes unscalable if you don't fix these issues. You have to be a manager and like think about the your own project and how it works. 

The other and probably more difficult part. AI doesn't have good taste. It can't like come up with a good game mechanic for you to use. You are still going to have to design the UI. It won't make good dialog. 

TLDR;

Even with AI. It's hard to make a good game worth buying. The quality of games are all going to increase because everyone has access to these tools. 

And marketing your game is still just as hard as it was before.

It will cost a lot of time. But the money barrier is going to go way way down.
